segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I thank you for coming in here. Starting off, tell me your English and Cherokee names, Roger first.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Roger Glass, “Lo-li” is my name in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What is it?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: “Lo-li.”

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Mike Glass, “Nu-i-da” is my name.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where were you born, Roger?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Tahlequah.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Tahlequah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Growing up, where?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Greasy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Tell me a little about growing up.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Mike first.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: As for myself, growing up as I remember, I still think about the way things were when I was a boy. I was thinking about it the other day. I don’t know how you would say it in Cherokee, but commodity they used to get, they used give away then. I was little. Every month we would go to get it, and bring it home in a barrel. I guess we were kind of well off, I thought, but I didn’t know we were poor. We were getting commodity, that I remember growing up. It seemed like we were missing nothing, I think. We had plenty to eat - potatoes, beans and grease, gravy and biscuits. That’s mostly what we ate, but as for myself, that was good. Nothing else was missing for myself. For meat, my dad went hunting. Then we had meat. If it wasn’t for that, we didn’t eat meat. Or sometimes, someone would give him hog meat. That’s the way it was as I was growing up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That canned meat, is that what you got?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, every time we got commodity, we ate that. But as for cow meat or hamburger meat, I didn’t know that. I was thinking about that a while back. First, I thought, we were picking beans, and then sometimes we would stop in town for a regular hamburger and Coke. That’s all I knew. Then later on, I went with Sam and Glorene. They took me with them to town, to that Dairy Prince or Dairy Queen, it used to be.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Just before you got into town?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, we stopped there. “How about you? What do you want?” they said. “Regular hamburger and Coke,” I said. “Nothing else you want?” said Sam. “I don’t know what else they have,” I said. I ate a steak sandwich. I didn’t know what else they had, all I knew was regular hamburger and Coke. Growing up, all I knew was the woods and fishing. I felt good about that for myself. Nowadays, they don’t have that.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: They didn’t have things like that then. We made what we played with ourselves then. What we wanted or seen somewhere. And we didn’t have television. I remember a man stayed with us for a while, Johnson Soap was his name. He stayed with us and he bought a television for us to watch, and he was blind.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He played piano, didn’t he?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, he played piano, he bought the television, a little one. He just wanted to listen to Grand Ole Opry. We’d watch sometimes, when it used to come on. We didn’t have electricity until I was nine. I was maybe 10 or 12 years old when we had put in. The night Joe Cason got done hooking it up and they turned it on, I almost went blind. It seemed real bright to me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you all live at that time?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: At that time, that turnoff at Starr Killer, “Do-k-see” turnoff.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: This side of that house?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Where them ponds are, that’s where the house was. We lived in one there, and the other further on belonged to the government. Just past Black Bridge, they called it, there was a house we lived in for quite a while, I remember.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it on past there at Starr Killer?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, just past it, it was.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That Ice lived close to you?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah. On further, soldiers stayed in what I think used to be Army barracks. They said we lived there, too, when I was three or four years old. I remember a little of when we lived there. One time I remember, though, we came home. I don’t know where we had been but we came home and the goats were in the house. They were on the bed. “U-da-so-d(i)” the late, walked by, grabbed one by the horns, drug it by us, and threw it outside. The goats were in the house, but at the time, they didn’t lock the doors.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: I don’t know how they opened the door, but they got in the house. I don’t remember much about when we lived there. I was too little then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That armadillo probably done that to get in. Where did you go to school?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Greasy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You finished?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, eighth grade.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: High school then?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Sequoyah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Play ball there?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, but I didn’t know anything. I played football, but I didn’t know what they were doing. I was learning, I thought. The first touchdown I made at the time, I remember, was a punt blocked by Richard Rider, and it landed where I was standing. I picked it up, the referee was standing there, and I was going to hand it to him. “Run, run!” he said.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Referee told you that?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, “run, run,” he told me. I scored that time. Didn’t even know what I was doing, but I scored. I didn’t know what I was doing, but I made touchdown, my first one. Didn’t know nothing, but learned a little then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: College, too?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Started. I tried at Bacone. After I quit, I thought about it later on.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, you can do that. Me, too, I’ve messed up twice. I went to school, then I quit. What did you do when you were working?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Mostly, you know, I worked in construction. Then I started in Stilwell where they made chairs and tables. I worked at Ft. Smith too, a few times, like Ayers & Garrison, and Ward’s.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Desoto.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Desoto, too, I worked there a little while. Then I started at Stilwell Foods canning factory. I worked there for 42 years.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When they used to bring strawberries, do they still do that, or have they quit that? Hey, somebody came in. Had they already quit, and them beans?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Nothing like that anymore. Just pies. They make cream pies, and okra, too. They make all of them (Cof-ga-lo-dol-disg).

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is what they call that, isn’t it? They still bring that okra, but it comes from a different place?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: It comes from Texas way, most of it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Roger, now.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Ah, mostly I grew up at Greasy, too. I remember, where he said they lived, that house was a log cabin. By Ice’s house, that turn-off is where we lived for a while. I was really little. “Mel” was a chicken, a really mean rooster. It would take after you when you were out. One time, I remember “Mel” got out. “Watch out for your sister,” Momma told me. I seen a chicken was running towards us, so I left “Mel” and it got on my sister. My dad came out, grabbed that rooster by the neck and threw it in the thicket. I was really little. I remember we moved to my uncle’s old house. That’s where I grew up. We didn’t live anywhere else. I remember that late uncle and late grandma. When we were little, my late grandpa would go to the store. He would buy Pepsi and he would have it in his pockets. When he showed up, “Hey,” he would say, “take them out of my pockets.” And while we were fighting over it, he’d drink them up. That’s how I remember my late grandpa. My late grandma would tell me about things. “When you grow up, boy,” she said one time, “don’t you make your blood mixed.” When I thought about it later on, I understood. Don’t marry a different race, she told me, don’t make it mixed with different blood.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: “You find Cherokee,” my dad would say.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what she was saying. I remember lots of things she used to tell me. And they would go someplace the elders were sitting, with that Mike outside they would be sitting talking about things. I think about it nowadays. At that time, they saw what was going to happen. “We will be paying for water,” they said. “It’s going to come, and there will be a light shining on a mountain someplace.” “Why would they know that?” I thought then. Today, you can see it on mountains, houses all over. “One couldn’t live there. They will have houses all over,” they would say. I don’t remember those old men that were sitting there. They would talk about a lot of things, and I would listen. “Sit down,” they would tell me, “and be quiet, too,” they would tell me. I would be crawling, finding some toy. I would be pushing it. I grew up Mom’s way. When playtime came, cowboys and Indians were all we knew. When the Killers came, we played cowboys and Indians. Hank, Mose and all would come Sunday or Saturday. We would play in the woods. Hank and him met.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: For real, we pretended when we fought.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Fighting in a beer joint, that’s what they done. They really fought, they weren’t just playing, they were trying to kill each other.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Falling around, fighting. We were fighting with fists.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Hit him on the back with a chair. We were laughing. Then, in a little while, they’d break them up. Really had to separate them. Somewhere they would meet up and be the same again. It was for real to them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: There was no need to make them mad?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: No, didn’t have to. We pretended fighting, we used fists fighting, but we missed, and they wouldn’t be missing, they’d be hitting each other.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That combat, did you all watch that?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I, too, liked watching it.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Later on, when we got the television, we watched it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, if one had that dish, they were still playing that.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Saturday nights, at nine, playing at that time.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: He was fighting the same way when we didn’t have lights, when we lived in the log cabin. Boy, it was dark, just the light – what do they call it? Coal oil. Put oil in it till it would give off a little light. It was dark in there. Then when we got to Mom’s, I don’t know why, the paint was sort of black at first, then later they painted the house green, dark green.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Found what someone threw away, probably.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Probably what they did. As for light, it gave off a little shine, and in the morning, we didn’t have water, we had a well, but...

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: A well was under the house.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: And it was deep.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That thing was about this long?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, there we got our water. People would stop sometimes; they came after water. They would get it there. We gave it to them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You talking about that one Florene’s close to?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you remember when they tore it down?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They left one wall.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: That well is still there. They covered it up, but still it’s there. They built flooring there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: This is what happened. They did that, and quickly they realized a new one has to be built, they said. But at the time, all they done is rehab. “We can’t build a new one,” they were told. That’s why they left one wall, rehab was all they were doing. Really, Bertha Allsmate thought about that. “Alright, let’s tear it all down, but leave one wall. We’re rehabbing it,” she said.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you work at?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: I worked at the canning factory, but not for very long. Then I went to Greenleaf. I don’t know if I was making $30 a week there then.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: It was my fault he got fired at Greenleaf. Went back, got his check. “’Lifetime, no rehire,’ they told me,” he said.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: But I didn’t care.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Really hot, it was.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: I didn’t like outside work. In Tulsa, I worked in construction. About this month it was, wasn’t it? Yeah, when June came, I quit that.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Myself, I liked that construction work.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Me too.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: I didn’t like it. Whatever job I could find is what I did.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Do you remember, in Tulsa, where we were working, that man was using that vibrator? I don’t know what his name was. He went and got that vibrator and plugged it in. It came on, 220v had been changed over and shocked him. He was laying there. Vibrated him, didn’t it?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, we went that way. “Don’t touch that, don’t touch that,” he was saying, just barely talking. I forgot what his name was.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: I don’t know what it is.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Didn’t it do anything to him?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: I don’t know. At the time, he was standing there trembling.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: He started talking, then he started trembling.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Almost killed him, that electricity.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: One time we went to work there, later on, we were sent to different areas. Ice was saying they were looking for Mike. He was somewhere deep. I guess a culvert was there.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, it was a culvert. It was small, box-like, and it was long. I was pulling boards there.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: There, he went to sleep. “Gah-lee,” said Ice, “he was snoring inside there.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He was crawling around in the mud?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Wagner had to do that, raking it out.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: You all had to do like that, too?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Don’t know what he found for bedding.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Passed out, maybe. That’s when you got fired, he was saying. The Dry’s that live toward Jay, one of them at Grove, he worked at furniture storage, but he got fired. He came to where his brother worked. “Huh, I got fired,” he said. “I was doing nothing, either,” he said. “Well, that’s how come they fired you,” I told him.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many were you in the family?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: As for me, my dad and myself was all, but a half-brother I have is living, named Jimmy. Also Peggy, a half-sister, and what’s his name? “I-sa-yi.”

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: That one is white.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: But he didn’t grow up around here. “To-tsu-wa” my half-brother was his dad. We’re kind of odd, our moms are sisters.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was that?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Our moms were sisters. His dad was my dad’s son, how would you say that? They were father and son.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That is odd.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Didn’t know if that was my nephew or just kin, but most people think we’re brothers, that’s what people say. I don’t say anything about that, if they say ‘your brother,’ that’s all. All the time, we were growing up together.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: They were talking about where they lived. Do you remember that log cabin they lived in? I remember. I’ve still got a scar here [gestures]. One time we were throwing some metal on top of a roof. When it came down, we’d catch it. He had that metal in his hand. “Want me to hit you with this?” he said. “OK,” I said to him. Boy, he cut me here [gestures], and I still got a scar to this day. He hit me on the head. “Want me to hit you with this?” he asked, and “OK,” I said. That I remember good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: All of you spoke Cherokee?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, ‘til later on we started learning English. I started school then. I learned most of it, but my uncle kind of taught me, too. He was trying to teach me what he knew when we lived at Rock Fence way. I was maybe five years old, I think then. About that time, my late uncle passed on. He was teaching us a little Cherokee. Still later, too, I watched that television. I don’t really know when I learned English, if you really tell about it, I don’t know. My brother’s late dad, “To-tsu-wa,” all the time hated me when I learned a little English. I didn’t want it to pass me by. Last time I was there, what I see showing, then I would be throwing around English, from what I was seeing. “Hah,” he would say. “That attorney is here again,” he would say, because I was speaking English.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Mostly, you all spoke Cherokee.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: That’s all, we spoke Cherokee.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Still, to this day, when we get together, we talk all Cherokee, nobody speaks English.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And you, how many in your family?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Eight, seven of us boys, and one girl.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Just one girl, was it?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You all, too, you all speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You now, where did you go to school?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Greasy, too, when I went. Don’t know how, but I got through eighth grade. I felt good eating.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How about high school, did you go to school?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: I went a little while, at Cave Springs. I went to school for three years. No, in my fourth year I quit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They not play football, then?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: No, they didn’t, baseball was all they had, but I did try that baseball. I didn’t have nothing, not even a mask. They wanted a hind catcher. “I’ll hind catch,” I told them. They made me shortstop, at first, when we first started, but I wanted to play hind catcher. I caught without a mask, and some time later, they found what used to be a mask. It didn’t have that padding on. How they put it on, I don’t know. They put it on with string or small rope, they tied it on. I put it on and was sitting there, when the batter tipped the ball and hit my mask. This big a mark was on my head here [gestures].

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Didn’t have no padding there?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, there. “Ding!” it went, or my head made that sound.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Myself, going to school in Thirsty, I think it was Windburg. “Boys, we got a ballgame tomorrow,” he said. First district game, we got knocked out.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Just your first game?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, Oaks, they made us look real bad.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: That, too. They kick the ball. We went to play somewhere, what was the name?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It wasn’t Arkoma, was it?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, we went there one time, just because I wanted to get out of class. “Anybody want to play soccer?” they said. I didn’t know what soccer was, but I raised my hand and the other boys raised their hands. “Come on,” he said, so we went and played, not knowing anything. We got beat there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That grandkid of mine plays that. I didn’t like it because I didn’t know how it went.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: My nephew was playing. I don’t understand how it goes, so I’d say to him, and that girl one, all the time her husband. I’ve never gone and watched, because I don’t know what they’re doing.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Me too. I went for the Minks but, “Hurry up and get done,” I was thinking.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was your parents’ name?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Fannie was my mother's name. George Jr, “To-tsu-wa” they called him, Redbird mostly.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, I remember that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And you?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: George T. Glass was my dad, “Da-so-d(i)” they called him, but his real name was “U-tlv-hen.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was that?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: “U-tlv-hen.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: “U-tlv-hen.”

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: That’s his real name, they say. I don’t know, but “U-da-so-d(i)” is what they called him. Go to sleep, sitting up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He is falling off.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: My mom, Mary was her name. Used to be Killer but now Glass, Mary Glass, her Cherokee name was Ke-ho-g(i) That Fannie was saying “Ge-di” her name in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Ice and Mary are immediate family?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, so is “Ge-di” or Fannie. She is in family, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, I didn’t know that.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: “Ge-di” is the only one left from the Killer side, isn’t it?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, the only one now.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I didn’t know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Still, do you sing, Roger?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Sometimes, on Friday night, we’ll have it, I think, there.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Friday.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Friday, I think at Fairfield.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Fairfield.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Mostly they sing in English there. I start them off in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You play guitar, don’t you?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Mike, too, you play guitar?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: No, I don’t know anything about it. I’ve forgotten a lot Cherokee songs, but I’m going to try to remember some. Not being there at the singing is why I have forgotten them, that’s why. I think it gets cut off nowadays for people to learn to speak Cherokee. Some are just singing. They can learn, they say, but they don’t say all we say when they sing.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: With some it is cut out. Some, when they sing, I don’t even know what they’re saying. But not hearing it is why I forget it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: For myself, that East Central, where I was pastoring, it was all white. That’s what was happening – I was forgetting the songs.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Myself, that’s what was happening. When I went Checotah way, I forgot a lot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you still preach?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Sometimes, mostly I go to the Indian Mission. Then the Creeks, they just give me a paper when they have services. The head man of that group, “Just whenever it comes to you, come and preach,” he said.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The Creeks way?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, Wewoka, Watonka, that way, and Okmulgee way.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You go there at times?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: I don’t go that way that much anymore, but I go sometimes to the Indian Mission. I help out mostly.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Who pastors there?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: No one.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Still, a good amount there?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, a few there, but not that many, mostly just a few family, now. It don’t come to me to pastor anywhere now. I don’t know why, I’ve done what I’m supposed to do, I think. I go different places just to help out.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s the way it is, myself. At first, when I started preaching, they would call me from all over. Then later on, it got still. “Why is that?” I thought, but I just prayed about it. Then later on, “It’s not as an evangelist I’m calling you for,” he told me. “I’m not calling you to pastor,” he said. Then I thought about it, but now, I don’t think nothing about it, if I don’t get called somewhere. Sometimes though, I get called and I’m thankful.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: I think, myself, just thinking about it, a little that way that evangelism is what I started at first when we went around singing. I believe in that way a little, I don’t know why. The Creeks’ way has been pulling me to help them out there. Some have been telling me, “You are different, but good. You’ve been telling us the right way,” they tell me in English. “You’re kind of different,” they tell me in English. Still, we have services if you go there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They don’t sing anymore?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: In the church they still sing, with the women on the right and the men on the left. Still that way, and that altar is open. We say they all gather; however many preachers there are, all of them will preach. They will call the young ones. When you get done talking, then you leave it open, and the altar will be this way [gestures], then they will put it up this way [gestures] like a mercy seat, I guess you call it, for people to come to eat.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that the Creeks?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, Creeks. When you quit, again they’ll put it up this way [gestures], then the second speaker comes up. When he’s done, they’ll do the same thing again. One time, I was there at the Creeks the first time. Not really the first time I went there, but it was that church. They were talking about something - they were going to blow the horn. I didn’t know what they were talking about. “What are they talking about?” I was thinking, and they were still eating. They’ve got buildings - each family’s house is where they eat, on their own, and one they call the common hall by itself is where they feed all people or visitors. And the families have their own houses where they eat. They were talking about doing that, then at two it was time for them to start. They stay there all day, then at two, about time to start church, “I’m going in,” I told them. So I went in and sat there. After a little bit, I heard something. It was that horn. My hair went up like this [gestures]. “Boy, I’m going now,” I was thinking. “Come back, Jesus,” I was thinking, looking around. For real, I’m not joking, nothing happened. I was thinking, standing outside, “What was it?” I was thinking. When it got quiet, about 10 minutes later, it went off again. Same thing happened, I was waiting to go up, but nothing happened. Later I realized, in the Old Testament tabernacle, first they blew the horn, letting people know it was time to gather and start, to get what they were saying ready. The second time it went off, people come in. Not just the Creeks could come in, but the inner court, they came in the church first, then the second time it went off, it was for all to come in. They still do the same there when they have services. I thought I had missed it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: “I got left behind,” you thought.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Somewhere, the church I was at, close to Stilwell is a church, Chalk Bluff. A woman from Africa was there. She had that kind of horn, a goat horn, she said it was. After a little while, she blew it. It sounded beautiful, but they didn’t say why she done that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Something like that bell they sound over here, was it?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, but she was blowing the horn, mostly.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Belfonte, where I pastor, Lee Sevenstar or Denny Soap will ring the bell when it came time. “Ring it,” they told me. I was standing there, and I broke it. “Don’t you touch it a second time,” they told me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Mike, that while ago, you was telling us what you had. Tell us.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Oh, the owl [Great Horned Owl] that I had, it was young when I caught it. First I was hunting, I knew squirrels used to be in a dead tree that had a small hole. They would go in there, so I shook it. That’s what came out and flew away. It hit a limb and fell in the water, that creek by the two stores where we lived then. I caught it then. I took it home with me and was feeding it, but it wasn’t eating much. I didn’t know what to feed it. I gave it just anything, a bird I gave it just starting, I kept it in a house a while like I was raising it. Boy, it kept getting meaner-looking when I got there to feed it. There I was, looking at it, it was getting meaner-looking and was looking right at me when I was looking at it. I got scared and let it out. Mean-looking it was. Then, I had a hoot owl. I caught that, too, it was the same, little. It came out of a tree and hit a limb, but its feathers were real soft. Not good grown yet, it could fly good yet. It landed by me and I caught it. I took it with me and raised it. I kept it a good while. It was good and tall - I didn’t know they got that tall. Two or three feet tall it was, it was big and had long wings. I raised it with just birds or rabbits. I would cut a piece of meat and give it to feed. That was weird, I had no idea when at first I noticed. When I fed it birds, about two days later, I would find bones laying around. “Why is this?” I thought. “What’s it doing?” I was thinking then. I kept a lookout, wondering when it passed it, that’s what came out, I was thinking. But at last I found out: when I fed it, it would be weird. When I gave it something, it would get on top of it and cover it up with its wing, cover its head with its wing. It would pick it up, start eating that bird, swallow it whole. Just then, I found out how they do that. When it eats, later it regurgitate and all the bones come out. I didn’t know that’s what they done with the bones. It would throw up the bones after the meat came off. I kept that owl for quite a while. It could fly then. I had a long rope or string I tied to its leg, and let it fly outside and fly around. The way I raised it up, it would walk around outside, then I would put back in a wire box I had. Then people found out that I was keeping it. Kids would sometimes bring sticks. They started jabbing it and making it mad, and when it got mad, they liked that. It would screech real loud and back up with its wings spread out, making that sound the kids liked. Sometime later, I just felt sorry for it, the way people had been bothering it, so I released it. I found a strip of leather and tied it to one leg, thinking later on I might see it somewhere. I thought so, but I haven’t.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Haven’t seen it?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: No, never have I seen it later on.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it hooting?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, but not while I was right there. When it was by itself, it would hoot, the way they sound but not that much. But while I was outside, I never heard it hoot. But I just let it go. I felt sorry for the way people bothered it. Still, people would come looking for it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Looking for it.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: I let it go, I did.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Do you remember, long time ago, the monkeys they caught at Greasy?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No, where was that?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: At close to Di-ga-no-tsa-tli [James Vann’s], they caught them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, yeah, now I remember.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: One was close to my house. My brother could see it. “That’s just a squirrel you’re seeing,” we’d tell him. “No, it’s a monkey,” he’d say. “No, it can’t be no monkey,” we’d say, us bigger kids. He was little. Later on, John Killer came. He looked. “There’s a monkey up there,” he said. Then we went out and ran after it, but it got away from us down the hill. Where Di-ga-no-tsa-tl(i) [James Vann] used to live, it went toward his old place. The dogs treed it there, and they caught it. Bob Duvall, I think, caught it. There they had it in a cage, too. Someone stabbed it and killed it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Huh.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Killed the monkey.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Who done that?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Joey, Bob’s boy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: He was stabbing it with a stick, making it mad. It just gave up, I guess.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where... did they ever find out where it came from?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: I don’t know. Maybe, they thought, trucks go by. Maybe it jumped out, they thought. There were three of them.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, three, I thought.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, three they were. That, too, White Oak Red caught one.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: They were real little, just yea big [gestures].

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It wasn’t a real little Bigfoot, was it?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: My mom one time went after some wild onion. She went downhill towards that dam. After a little while, she came back. “What’s wrong?” I said. She was real scared, boy. “I seen a bird that was huge or something,” she said. “I don’t know what it was, but it had feathers. But its head was not a bird’s,” she said, “it was something else,” she said. “A buzzard, probably,” I said. “A dead cow was laying there,” she said, “and it would go inside there,” she said, “put its head inside. I got to it real close. When it came out, it was this high and about this big,” [gestures] she said. “What was it, do you think?” I said. “I don’t know, never have I seen something like that,” she said. “You were just imagining it,” I told her. “No, I really seen it,” she said. Sometime later, they said that an emu had gotten out.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: That’s what was feeding on that cow laying there. “It’s inside.” I thought something was wrong with my mom, but then they said, “You know that DJ who had that field close to school? It was running like that,” they said.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They released them. They said they were valued a lot, but their eggs weren’t worth nothing, so they released them, they said.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Myself, one time, where Rick Williams lived, straight away there, we were running it down in our auto. In a little while, I looked to the side, and it was running alongside us. It was fast, running alongside. I don’t know where it came from, then it went off away. It was racing us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: My house, that old one we lived in, they released one close to it. Sometimes, still, it would make something like a humming noise. We heard, but we never knew what it was till later, down the hill, Jim Vann caught one. That’s what it was doing, moving like this, it would hum. He caught one though, Jim. Don’t know what he done with it.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: You all talk about that. I didn’t see it myself, just them talking about it, that Gene Breen had them Rottweilers. He took them to be mean. They were mean-looking dogs. One got my leg one time, but at that time, he had the dogs penned. When they came back, Donovan himself was telling it, that Albert Vann came back. They said they were trying to catch it, the dogs were. He said, “Boy, it was really whipping them dogs,” he said. It was whipping them mean Rottweilers. “Didn’t sit too well with Gene,” he said, “whipping his dogs.” They were trying to catch it, chasing it, but they didn’t catch it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It will kick you hard, they say.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: That’s what they say.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I wouldn’t let it.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: I could never catch it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Mike, did your dad ever mention that Trail of Tears? Anything that included him?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: No, I don’t remember him talking anything about that. What he talked about, I remember how they came. I don’t know if it’s true about our late uncle, Ned Longbird was his name. They say, I don’t know if you have heard the same, he was just a little boy, and he was in it, they say. When they got here that time, I don’t know if it’s true, who was it? Someone we asked to look that up, at North Carolina, the names of people that left there. Not anybody with Longbird name was in it, that time, but later people that search stuff like that, maybe Talala way, arrived then. They came this way, maybe it was too many people. Bird was last name, cause he was tall, wasn’t he?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, I had seen him.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Because he was tall, maybe they gave him the name of Longbird and then it was changed. Ned Longbird was his name. Maybe that’s why they can’t find the name Longbird. Where do they come from, they say, people would tell that, don’t know if it’s true, that’s all I heard them talking, that he a little boy then they arrived here. That’s all I know.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: He was born on their way here, I think.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, he was born on their way here.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Ohh.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: He was born on their way here, they said, is all I know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Me too. I heard just recently that my late dad was just a little kid when he was a part of that, they say. If I had known that, at first, I would have asked him about it, if he had seen it.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: The elders used to meet, don’t know for what purpose, I was too little then. “Where did you go?” they ask each other, Cherokee the Old, they would say. Was that what they were talking about, how and what happened over there, or did they go all the over there? I would think, “I don’t know, I was too small.” “Where you been?” they would say, Cherokee the Old. They would just say, “Don’t know.” Maybe that’s what they were talking about. I thought, “What happened there?” I thought at the last, a while back, “Where are they going, Cherokee the Old?” I was saying. I didn’t know where that was.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Have you all been there?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: No, I haven’t been there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Have you?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That they call Cherokee, you been there?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, Indians were dancing in the street, just two were dancing, and a bear. I went and looked at it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: This next month, halfway through, two weeks you going to be there, isn’t it?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what they said. It’s a good place to go, I thought.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: A few times we have been there. Five-O was preaching there, at Hillside. I was pastoring then, the boy singers were helping him, and I went with them. Three years we stayed there. I was scared of them mountains.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Deep down, you can look there, there’s one with a curvy road you can take to Smoky Mountains, they said. I don’t know the way things are there. I was just riding and they would tell how things were. We were driving along and stopped at a roadside there. I was dropping rocks off it. Later, I thought if there was a road below, I could hit someone, I thought. It just went silent when I dropped a rock.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Or someone’s house.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: We were moving that John Flute over there. He was going to pastor, and we went along. On a mountain bluff there was a trailer. We were still yet a lot higher and above us, rocks would slide off. “Maybe you’d see it if you’re walking around,” said one of them. “Might be a bear walking there. That’s what it does when there’s a bear walking,” he said. “God,” I said, “John, a bear is going to come after you. Another bear, he’s going to think of you,” I told him.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you like it while you were there?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, it was a good place to go. That Emma Smoke or Smoker, what’s her name?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, Smoker.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: That’s who kept us there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what they’ll do, if you go there. For us, first time we went, first year, we slept on that church floor. That one, John West was his name, lived over there. We became friends. Then the second year we went there, “You’re not going there this time, you all are going to my house,” he said.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: She was saying, a lot of people have been there, she said, at her house. There were pictures hanging, and that Teehee boy was with us. “Golly, Tom Slick,” he said, “who’s Tom Slick?” I thought it was Tom Grayson picture hanging there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That what I said, John West, breakfast, noon, and supper, he feeds us.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what they do, real early in the morning, they’re rattling the pots and pans, or frying pan. In the morning you’d hear them. When you got out of bed, wouldn’t be nobody around. It was their kids that came real early to cook, they would be talking, but I didn’t want to go in there. When I got up I’d go in there, it would be just the old lady there eating, waiting on us to get up. It was that long, a week, we would be there, for a week they would feed us. “When you all leave, we’ll start donating money for next year, for us to feed you all when you all come back,” he said. That’s what he would do.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: He was prepared.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He had goats. He would rent them for the brushes.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Real quick, they would clear it out.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what they done, he’d fence them with just electric wire, and put them in it. As big an area as they wanted, he would fence it and put them in. Later, when it was done, he would take them back.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Real quick, they can clear it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what he said. “A lot have quit using dozers,” he said. I wondered why. I thought, “Are they eating up the big trees?” I thought.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: There are houses just about all the bluffs.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, you have to go up to get there.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: I’ve just heard people talking about it. The fluent Cherokee speakers are just a few up that way. “Is it true the real speakers live in the woods and the mountains?” is what they say.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When we had services, they didn’t come, there at Cherokee where we were, but that’s the way it is, only about 150 are there now, speaking Cherokee. Myself, I couldn’t really understand them talking, and it’s different, too. I don’t remember just how they say “Di-g(a)-tu-le-na” (car or truck). What we say, they don’t say it that way. I think, just as we say “Tsi-le-li” (gum), they say different.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: They say “Di-dla” (with rubber tires), wasn’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s it, maybe.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: “A-tsv” is they say, for “A-dla” (rubber). They don’t have the “tl” sound as they speak, as “dla, tla, tle, tli, tlo, tlu, tlv.” They use “tsa, tse, tsi, tso, tsu, tsv,” and it changes the sounds. Like we say “A-tla,” they say “A-tsv.”

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Different areas got different dialects, that woman was telling me. She said where it was, real nasty they talk, she said. “Sit over here, (A-h(a)-ni, Tso-tle-s-di) we say. (A-h(a)-ni, ha-nv-ga) they say,” she said, “you go farther down. They talk nasty, (A-h(a)-ni, ha-sa-la-tla-he-s-di) what they say,” she said, “isn’t that nasty?” she said. That’s what I would say, I told her.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s just the way it is now, isn’t it?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s the way it is.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Us now, a nasty time we live in.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s the way they are, nasty they talk, she said. This one, what was his name uhh, Mark it was, Mark Brown I think he said his name was, don’t know if he’s still living. He came to Stilwell, came to visit me. “Are you singing in Cherokee?” he said. “I’ll give it a try,” I told him. “They say you have recorded some,” he said. “Yeah, I have some,” I told him, and I gave him one. “I’m going to take it back there with me,” he said. He got back with it, no doubt. Then, someone else came from California way, and he asked for one. Again, I gave him one; he didn’t speak Cherokee that one, but the other one, he spoke Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Just wanted to hear them?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, lots of places we’ve been singing in Cherokee, they ask for them and don’t understand them. “Why, same as Mexicans singing. I don’t want to listen to them.” The white people like to hear Cherokee, they say. “I don’t know, we don’t understand them but you all make it sound good,” they say. “You all don’t know what we’re saying?” I told one, “We might be saying something different. We just make it up if we forget,” I told them. He laughed. “We wouldn’t know anyway,” he said. They wouldn’t know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Last time, where Doris works, she took some. “Come with us,” she said, so I went with them. “I’d like to go to the services in Cherokee,” I told them. So, let’s go we said, I want to hear them singing in Cherokee I said. I had to start them off. Five was all that was there, then. “You can preach, too,” he said. “White person, too, that was pastoring. Go head and preach,” I was telling him. Yeah, I had to start them off, and I was wanting to listen to them singing.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Me too. “I’m going to hear something different,” I thought when we went there. Not just myself singing, they told me, so I sung there.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: That, too, Mika, they all went there, that choir she was in. Traditional Cherokee food, they said, so we went to eat. “Lots of chicken on the table,” she said. We got done eating, and out the back, KFC boxes were piled up. She said, “Yeah, after we were done, we seen empty KFC boxes piled up,” she said. One time he brought Five-O, that one. “I like to watch how people eat and what they eat, all kinds of people,” he said. “I’m just curious sometimes. They get mad at me, but that’s the only way you’re going to learn something,” he said. This one time, he brought a young girl. I asked her, “What do you like to eat?” I said. “What do you all eat there in North Dakota?” No, she was from South Dakota. “Sonic,” she said. I was wanting to know what to cook for her. “Sonic,” she said. Probably wouldn’t have liked it if I had had hog meat. I get amazed at people. They ask me sometimes, “What does squirrel taste like?” they say. “Squirrel?” I say. “For me, nothing different I know of,” I tell them. “That’s just way we ate growing up. We didn’t know Sonic,” I tell them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I didn’t like squirrels, but I liked rabbits. There aren’t that many anymore, are they?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: No, you can’t find very many.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But squirrels, there’s a lot of them around.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: With Ann, we hunted them all the time. It’s been around three or four years since we hunted. That’s what we hunted the summer through. On Thanksgiving, we’d get together. I’d make dumplings. I’d use squirrels in my cooking, cut them all up first. Then I started watching that Duck Dynasty. When they had squirrels, they would just cut them in half and put them in. “So, that’s all you do,” I told them, and I started doing them that way, just cut them in half and toss them in.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Not nowadays does anyone hunt squirrels. That’s why there are so many of them.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Myself, I’m going to start back, this June thirtieth. I’m going to retire from working - that’s what I plan anyway, right now. Then they’ll be hollering, them squirrels, from being scared of me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where do you work, now?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Swann’s.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Still there?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, 42 years I’ve been working there.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: You talking about squirrels, I remember one time when we had dinner at the church, Bob brought squirrels with dumplings. Ruby Poor, did you know her?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Who was that?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Ruby Poor.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, Ruby Poor, yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: She was cooking, with the bones still in. Then the white people came. “What’s that?” they were saying. “Squirrel,” she told them. “I’m not going to eat that,” they were saying. Going by that, us Cherokees were tearing it up. Then later, Bob said, “Ruby, next time I bring you squirrels, take the meat off,” he told her. She did that the second time. She had them on the table when they came by. “What’s that?” “Oh, that’s just meat,” she told them. Then they tore up the squirrels.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When Dirthrow was living, in Chester, Arkansas, we were cooking hog meat. Don’t know if it was Memorial Day or not, but it was some holiday. We’d go cook it, and those white people would come over and look at it, and make a face. When it came time to eat, they would tear it up at the table.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: One time, when we got to Hank’s house, they had fish on table, perches. A plate full they had caught, they had on the table. “Come eat,” they said. Right away, we went in there and tore them up. They were sitting and taking the meat off the fish and eating it. Before we knew it, we had eaten all of them, with just bones piled up. We ate all of the fish. As I was growing up, I remember when I ate fish, they would hand me one. “Bones, watch out for bones,” they would say. “If it gets stuck in your throat, just swallow a piece of biscuit.” That’s just the way I grew up, they didn’t piece it off for me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it perch?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, it was perch.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They’re really good to eat. There were a lot in the creek. Mom used to fry them good. She’d eat them, bones and all.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Crispy fried.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s the way she would do, or we done them.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Us, if it was perch, we ate head and all.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what we did.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: My wife, I told her that. “And you like fish,” I asked her, right after we got married. “Yeah, I love fish,” she told me. They had told me they were going to cook fish. We got there, and sitting there, she was watching them. “Aren’t you going to cut the head off? I can’t eat it when the fish is looking at me,” she said. “It’s dead,” I said. She got a paper towel, covered its head, and pinched the meat off.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What Cherokees eat, does she eat like that?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Used to, but her going to the doctor, and the medicine they give her sort of messes up her stomach. She can’t eat that much, just yogurt mostly, hamburger once in a while. But yeah, she would eat like us, some, not all. Crawdads she could really eat.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you all catch crawdads?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Just all over, any creek they were in. Sometimes at night, gigging them.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Boy, that’s what we used to do, and gigging for fish. Gigs we’d go by and pick them up. Really, the only reason they took us with them to the creek was to carry gigs. They would take the gigs from us.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: We would carry the light, and bugs were bad biting us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Winter, was it?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Summer, too, we done it then. Over at, what they call it? Bradly Ford we would start from, wading the creek, by the cemetery, and we would come to Rock Fence. Come all the way by creek gigging fish. I really liked doing that after I learned. One time, I started gigging fish after I learned, there close to Line Switch, we found red horses. A lot of them were in there. A gig is all I used to carry around, and I threw rocks around to make the fish go a certain way. I walked around, and this one time, there was a tree leaning over the creek. I climbed it and I was on it as the fish came by. I would gig them. “Da-sod-di” the late was standing a-ways, and they weren’t getting there, where he was snagging them. “Get off up there!” he hollered at me. “You’re scaring the fish away.” He made me get off that tree, so he could snag some he wanted.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You used that three prongs?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, he made me get off where I was. I was doing right, I thought, gigging fish, but he made me get off.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: As you all were growing up, when you got sick, did you use medicine from the doctor, or from the woods?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: We got it from the woods, and sometimes, years ago, when it came winter, Wattenburger, his name, wasn’t it, or Doctor Blue, one or the other.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Wattenburger, it was.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Doris talks about Wattenburger.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: He was at Bunch.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: You know where Roger lived, the corner at the bend, that house, that’s where he lived. Sometimes he would come and take us with him, and we’d go get a shot. Boy, I was scared when he went got the needle. It was big and all metal. To give us a shot, he’d use same needle, but he would clean it. I seen him do that - he would use just one needle.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: All rusted, probably.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: After he gave you a shot, he’d clean it with rubbing alcohol, what he used to clean it, then the second one he’d stick, boy, that was painful, as I remember, and on my cheek, this one hurt.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Myself, I ran away. He got that shot. “It’s quick. You get up there,” he told me.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: I was showing him where they stuck me.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Me, they had to catch.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You loved your cheek.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Didn’t have enough cheeks, myself. I never liked getting shots.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you all remember the kind of medicine they used, or knew?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: “Da-so-d(i)” the late used to hunt medicine like that. He did that all the time. When I think about it, it would have been good if we had paid more attention to that. He would take me along to the woods, hunting for medicine, digging up roots sometimes, then some wood bark. But he had to face a certain way at times, when he took them off. Roots were the most he knew about medicine like that. He’d have it hanging all different, for people with diarrhea, fever, and all different things people got sick with. He had medicine for someone with heart trouble. It was just a small root, but really bitter. I don’t know what it was called, but he called it “A-da-wi.” Two different kinds: “A-da-wi” that had one leaf, that and “I-wi” had two leaves. But nowadays, I couldn’t recognize it if I saw it. You could find it only on certain days. The rest of time, you couldn’t find it, really. You could find it just the days it came up. When he was teaching me, he had that stuff, really bitter it was.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Had to be boiled?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, a little bit of the root put in water, just a little piece put on your tongue.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Mom had some hanging, what he’s talking about, just a small stick. I don’t know how big it was. “Put it in your mouth,” she’d tell me. Phew, it was bad. My grandma used to treat me. I don’t know if you remember how it was. Her fingers were big and hard as rocks. She used hot coals. She’d go like this [gestures], seemed like she was touching fire. Where you were hurting, she’d put her hands on and it would burn.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: But it helped you all?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: I remember that as it was going on. But I can’t say it’s true, it scares people - what do they call rainbow in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: “U-qwo-la-tv.”

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: “Don’t point at a rainbow,” she would say. “How come?” I said to her. My late grandma, she pointed her finger at it. “You’ll lose it,” she told us.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: One time, I was standing there. “Don’t point at it,” she said. I used to point at it, and she said, “Don’t.” “Is that how come you’re so ugly?” I said to her. I got a whupping.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: In Nebraska, we used to go hunting. At times, the head man would come. One time, we had a fire going, a big fire, then they came. I knew he was drinking. Now and then, he’d get up and go to his pickup truck. Our fire would sometimes roll off. You know, that’s what it was doing, and when it done that, he’d get up and with his hand, just pick up the coal and put it back. He done that a few times. Sometimes it would be about this big [gestures], and he would just pick it up and put back on the fire. Then, I was a little scared of him. “What is that, sitting there?” I started thinking.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: My grandma would do that, too, like a hot coal dropped out of our stove, and she would pick it up by hand and put it back.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what he was doing. I was wondering if he was that drunk, but didn’t seem like it. We were talking good. A funny thing happened to him one time. Roger used to make knives and they brought the handles with them. They started talking about the knives, and after a while it came to him. “My momma gave one to me,” he said, and started crying.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: At this time, talk about whatever things come to you, or whatever you want. I’m going to leave it open - talk about anything you want.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Myself, one time something funny happened. I didn’t think it was real, but it really happened. All the time that “Da-sod” the late, I didn’t call him Dad. “Da-sod” was his name as I grew up. All the time we’d go in the woods, every time we would go by this kind of little bluff, “Don’t ever go there,” he’d tell me. He wouldn’t tell me why, he just said don’t go that way. Then later, what happens as you’re growing up, I wonder why he was trying to keep me from going there. I have to check why, I was thinking. Then I went and took the dogs with me. They started barking that way. “Here’s my chance,” I thought, and I went. I was looking around and it was getting late, close to getting dark. I got there, and the dogs were going around and barking. I looked towards the tree. One was a good squirrel-treeing dog. I looked, but that tree didn’t have many limbs. “How come there’s nothing on that tree?” I thought. I started getting on to them dogs. As I was getting on to the dogs, in a little while I looked down. There was a rattlesnake this tall [gestures]. It was standing, and its head was going this way and that way. With them dogs going round and round, it was this big in all [gestures]. I was standing downhill from it, and when I saw it doing that, I ran away this way, I don’t know why. I went uphill. “Might slow it down if it chases me,” I thought. I was standing there watching the dog. It wasn’t really trying to bite the dog, but just moving side to side. The dogs were circling it - really good dogs we had at the time. If I told them to stop they would stop, so I told them to stop and called them back, and they sat behind me, and that rattlesnake was still standing up, it was about this tall standing up there. Its body looked like it was this wide [gestures]. I was watching it. “What am I going to do?” I was thinking. In a little while, I shot at it and hit it in the neck just below its head. It dropped, and its head was this big [gestures]. The dogs jumped on it then. “What am I going to do now?” I was thinking. I took my belt off and put it around its head, wrapped it around its head, and I was dragging it. Still, I was jumpy, walking back. Then walking back someplace, it was brushy, leafy and sticks laying around. I stepped on one, and it came up and hit me. When it hit me, I jumped a ways, and when I landed, that snake landed right by me. Again I jumped, again it landed right by me. “That Blackbeer’s,” I was saying - you know where that’s at, don’t you?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: There on the other side, I came from there. Still, about three times I done that. I started running and when I turned around it was right behind me. Still I was running into limbs, my arms hitting them, and where we lived, what’s their names that live there, by the road and they sell wood that lived there? I forgot their names, we lived there then. From Blackbeer, I ran in the woods, I skinned up my knees, arms, and my forehead running into the limbs. As I turned around, right by me it landed. Then the road where we used to go over, there’s a house close to it. I came out there to the roadway. It was still woody then, people hadn’t moved in yet. I was running and my chest felt like it was going to explode. It was burning. “I have to do something,” I thought. “I’m going to kill it, or it’s going to kill me,” I thought. I turned around. Just then, I thought about that gun I was carrying. It’s a wonder I didn’t lose it while I was running. Just then I remembered I had a gun. “Guess I’m going to have to shoot it,” I thought. I stopped and turned. Then I realized I was dragging that snake, boy, I killed a huge rattlesnake that time, but myself, I liked to kill running away from it. I was dragging that snake. When I got there, boy, just barely got my breath back, when I realized that I was dragging it. “What am I going to do?” I thought. I cut off the rattles and took them with me. I was proud of myself. I told “Da-sod,” “Look what I killed!” He got onto me bad. He had been there already, that’s where they lived. That’s why he told me don’t go there, for that’s where they lived. “IS THAT WHERE YOU WENT?” he asked loudly. He got onto me, he did.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: It was level there, wasn’t it?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, badly. I ran from there, almost killed myself. I think I kept them rattles in the house, I don’t know, but the saying was, long time ago, “Sometimes thunder will hit them,” they say, “where the snakes live.” Dirt would slide down where they live. I kept the rattles in the house, but they found it and threw it outside. “Did you want lightning to hit our house?” I was told, and they threw it outside.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Rog now, tell us something.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: What he was telling is true, because we used to go over there. Black squirrels were there, too. There were holes where we found them, and we were throwing rocks, and down there deep, the snakes would rattle. And the smell, that’s what they smelled like. I just tagged along and he took me there one time. We didn’t understand nothing. Anything they told us not to do, we were going to do it.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: We were happy for something like that.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, we climbed trees all the time. We would bow it down, and put someone on it. We’d let it go and one of us would be hanging on.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: We’d jump from one tree to another tree.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We done that, too, hang on one tree and grab on to another.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Then, too, we would cut through the grapevines, and swing on them like monkeys, act like Tarzan.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Coming to the end, I ask, the way we speak Cherokee, what’s going to happen, do you think?

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Myself, I’m afraid this language we’re speaking, we’re going to lose it. The way that we speak we’re going to lose it, some or a lot of the things we say or pronounce. Things like say, if we come to someplace, “Jo-ga-dil” - how you say that? “Ge-a-dil,” have you ever heard that? “Jo-ga-dil” like creek water going away, “Ge-a-dil” is water coming down. People, they’re going to lose how we say things like that. They won’t know that. Myself, I have to think about what is “S-kwon-dil” - the other side of the creek. A long time ago, when I was little, I remember “Da-sod” the late used to say that. “Ge-a-di-li” “Ge-a-di-li.” I didn’t know what that was, till later I learned. When you throw rocks, I was the one carrying rocks and chasing the red horse. He was telling me that’s where the fish were, and for me to go down that way and chase them back upstream. Like that, I believe we’re going to lose it, and the reason why is we don’t use it much. Then, too, nobody would understand it, only the ones behind us growing up. Then the ones trying how to say things, that I’m afraid of. I try to remember how to say things the old way. I teach Mika how to say things like that. I tell her or ask her if she’s ever heard things like that, when we talk. Myself, that’s what makes me a little leery that we’re going to lose that, the old language. Like we were saying a while back, “Ta-li-jo-si-ne” nowadays twenty-second, they would say, as I remember, “Ta-li-jo-ne, Jo-a-jo-ne, Nv-gi-jo-ne, Hi-s-gi-jo-ne”. That’s how I count. Somebody teaching that “Jo-a-jo-ne, Nv-gi-jo-ne”, you know, they don’t know what that is.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Old, that is.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s the old language. As for myself, I want it, but then I have to find someone to talk to and understand what I’m talking about. Then we can talk about things. If it’s not that way, then to heaven it goes, and nobody gets help from it. If I keep it to myself and I’m the only one that knows it, nobody is going to get help from it. That is why I believe we’re going to lose a lot of that. As for myself, don’t know about Rog.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: The same with me, a lot of things are disappearing, like the medicine. They said the farmers and ones has cattle, they’re killing the plants in some places. I think, when they spray the medicine and the roots, that way, too, we’re going to lose it. That’s what I tell them, but I guess out in the woods you can find it, if we know what we’re looking for. As for myself, I never learned how to tell what it looks like. They used to tell me when I was little, but I guess I was too hard-headed to learn.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Didn’t pick it up?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: No, I didn’t.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: As I think about it, no reason to, is what I thought.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: No real reason to.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: “If I was a medicine man,” I used to say, as my late grandma took me into the woods, but I was too little, I would rather play around.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Something I’m going to ask you, how would you say wall?

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: I have never found anybody that knew what it was.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Same.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Ceiling, neither.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: One person said, “S-qwa-du-lv”.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: “U-s-qwa-du-lv,” that I have heard, but I wasn’t sure.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I’m not sure either.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: “U-s-qwa-du-lv,” ‘side’ is what it means.

segments.speaker: mike-glass
segments.translation: Same as a siding you put on. As for myself, it’s right. I can’t say it’s like something already there, and you put a side to it. That’s the way I see it. If somebody said that to me, “U-s-qwa-du-lv,” something already there, then you put something up for the side, is the way I see it and what I think.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Same as you said, I don’t know what it is.

segments.speaker: roger-glass
segments.translation: Something with a roof, they would say, isn’t that so? Not what’s on outside.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I thank you for coming. It would be good, if we had more time.
